pages.title: Title
pages.summary: Asset Pricing Tests — testing the CAPM in the cross-section and the time series.

pages.title: What this deck covers
pages.summary: TOC: testable implications; Roll's critique; Fama–MacBeth (1973); practical data issues; FF92 (is beta dead?); GRS (1989); FF93 multifactor; takeaways.

pages.title: Recap: the CAPM equation
pages.summary: Sharpe–Lintner: E[ri]=rf+βi(E[RM]−rf) — risk premium = risk × price of risk. Black zero-beta version: E[ri]=E[Rz]+βi(E[RM]−E[Rz]). Big question: do average returns follow the linear E–β relation?

pages.title: The CML and the SML
pages.summary: Panel A: CML in σ-space — only efficient portfolios on it; securities 1–4 plot inside the frontier on iso-beta lines. Panel B: SML in β-space — ALL assets collapse onto the line. Total risk = systematic + idiosyncratic; beta = systematic only.

pages.title: Total vs systematic risk
pages.summary: σi² = βi²σM² (systematic) + σ²(εi) (idiosyncratic). β = Cov/Var. Same E[r] can pair with different total σ, but must share β. What prices is covariance, not variance.

pages.title: Intuition behind the CAPM
pages.summary: High-β assets pay off when you least need money (market booms) ⟹ must offer high E[r]; low-β assets hedge. Huge-variance zero-covariance asset: E[r]=rf — variance washes out in a diversified portfolio.

pages.title: Four testable implications
pages.summary: (1) E–β linear; (2) β is the only risk that matters; (3) E[RM]>E[Rz]; (4) with rf, E[Rz]=rf. Excess-return regression rit−rft=αi+βi(RMt−rft)+εit: αi=0 (time-series test); β captures the cross-section (cross-sectional test); premium positive.

pages.title: Testing the Black version
pages.summary: Raw-return regression rit=αi+βiRmt+εit; αi=E[Rz](1−βi) for all i; β captures the cross-section; E[Rm]−E[Rz]>0.

pages.title: Roll's critique
pages.summary: Only ONE genuinely testable hypothesis: the market portfolio is mean–variance efficient — everything else follows from it. In-sample, betas against any ex-post efficient portfolio produce the linear relation by construction. Proxy problem: proxy can be efficient when true market isn't (and vice versa), so rejection is ambiguous.

pages.title: How sensitive are inferences to the proxy?
pages.summary: Stambaugh (1982): inferences similar across proxies adding bonds/real estate — critique not empirically fatal. Kandel–Stambaugh/Shanken (1987): if Corr(proxy,true)>0.70, rejection with the proxy implies rejection with the truth. Jagannathan–Wang (1996): labor capital helps — critique may matter after all.

pages.title: A note on time: the CAPM is static
pages.summary: Maintained assumption for tests: returns MVN and iid through time; CAPM holds period by period; time averages estimate expectations. Despite rejections, CAPM stays useful: cost of capital, Jensen's alpha, event studies.

pages.title: The Fama–MacBeth cross-sectional regression
pages.summary: At each t: rit = γ1t + γ2t·βi + ηit across stocks. Average γ̂1t vs rf; average γ̂2t vs the premium. Augmented: add γ3·βi² (linearity) and γ4·σ(εi) (idiosyncratic risk); CAPM null: E[γ3]=E[γ4]=0.

pages.title: Step 1: time-series regression per asset
pages.summary: For each i: rit−rft = αi + β̂i(Rmt−rft)+εit. Save β̂i and σ̂²(εi); stack into vectors. Beta is estimated, not observed ⟹ errors-in-variables later.

pages.title: Step 2: the cross-section and the nulls
pages.summary: r̄ = γ1·1 + γ2·β + γ3·β² + γ4·σε² + η. Four nulls: E[γ1]=rf; E[γ2]=E[RM]−rf>0; E[γ3]=0; E[γ4]=0. Test by time-averaging monthly γ̂s with t-stats.

pages.title: Portfolio interpretation of each γ
pages.summary: Expand E[Rp]=Σwi·E[ri]: coefficients on rf, premium, γ3, γ4 are Σwi, Σwiβi, Σwiβi², Σwiσεi². Choose w so one sum =1 and the rest =0: each γ̂ is a characteristic portfolio return.

pages.title: Each γ is a minimum-variance characteristic portfolio
pages.summary: γ̂1: min w'Vw s.t. w'1=1, w'β=0, w'β²=0, w'σε²=0 (zero-beta); γ̂2: unit-beta zero-cost; γ̂3, γ̂4 analogous. OLS fitted values decompose average returns into these portfolio returns.

pages.title: The time series of cross-sectional regressions
pages.summary: One cross-section per month t=1..T; collect slopes; FM estimate γ̄2=(1/T)Σγ̂2t with s.e. = (1/√(T−1))·√((1/T)Σ(γ̂2t−γ̄2)²).

pages.title: Why average the slopes?
pages.summary: One big regression of time-averaged returns on betas gives the numerically identical slope, but OLS s.e. assumes independent residuals across assets — false (common shocks) ⟹ s.e. biased down, t-stats overstated. FM fix: each month's slope is one draw; cross-correlation absorbed into slope variation; monthly slopes ≈ serially independent. Caveats: autocorrelation, EIV.

pages.title: Practical data issues
pages.summary: Microstructure (non-synchronous trading biases thin-stock betas; bid–ask bounce ⟹ spurious negative autocorrelation; discreteness). Errors-in-variables ⟹ attenuation. Regression phenomenon: extreme β̂s revert to 1; sort first, average within portfolios.

pages.title: EIV in detail
pages.summary: β̂=β+e. Cross-sectional slope γ̂2 = Cov(r,β)/(Var(β)+Var(e)) — attenuation toward zero as Var(e) grows. Exactly the wrong direction for test power.

pages.title: Mitigating EIV: portfolios first
pages.summary: β̂i ~ N(βi, σ²(εi)/(T·σM²)); reduce noise by more T or diversification. Portfolios shrink residual variance ⟹ tighter β̂p. Trade-off: grouping also shrinks Var(β), the spread needed to identify γ2 ⟹ sort to maximize β-spread, then average.

pages.title: FF92: the indictment
pages.summary: On trial: (1) E–β positive and linear; (2) β suffices. The anomaly list: size (Banz 1981), leverage (Bhandari 1988), BE/ME (Stattman 1980; Rosenberg-Reid-Lanstein 1985), E/P (Basu 1983). Ball (1978): all are scaled-price ratios.

pages.title: FF92 headline findings
pages.summary: Beta is dead: average returns not positively related to β; β doesn't capture the cross-section; size + BE/ME do, and absorb leverage and E/P. Key move: independent variation in β and size via double sorting.

pages.title: FF92 data and sample
pages.summary: Non-financial NYSE/AMEX/NASDAQ, CRSP×Compustat, 1962–89. 6-month accounting–return gap (fiscal t−1 data, returns from July t). BE/ME and E/P use December ME; size uses June ME. Selection: price at June t & Dec t−1, ≥24 of past 60 months.

pages.title: Estimating betas without confounding β and size
pages.summary: June of t: 10 size deciles (NYSE breakpoints), then 10 pre-ranking-β portfolios within each ⟹ 100 portfolios. Full-period post-ranking betas with a lagged-market term (sum betas, non-synchronous trading fix). Stocks inherit their portfolio's beta.

pages.title: FF92 Table I
pages.summary: Panel A returns: read down — size effect strong (Small-ME all 1.52%/mo vs Large-ME 0.89). Read across within size — β varies (0.87→1.72 post-ranking) but returns barely move (All row: 1.34 low-β vs 1.14 high-β). No β–return relation independent of size.

pages.title: FF92 Table III: FM regressions
pages.summary: Avg slopes (t): β alone 0.15 (0.46) — dead. ln(ME) −0.15 (−2.58). β+size: β flips −0.37 (−1.21), size −0.17 (−3.41). ln(BE/ME) alone 0.50 (5.71). Size+BE/ME: −0.11 (−1.99) and 0.35 (4.44). BE/ME kills leverage; size kills E/P. 7/63–12/90, ~2,267 stocks/mo.

pages.title: FF92 conclusions and the open question
pages.summary: No β–return relation once size-independent β variation is used; ln(BE/ME) captures leverage; size+BE/ME capture E/P; robust across subperiods. Open question: rational (state-variable risk) vs behavioral (mispricing) story for size and BE/ME.

pages.title: Time-series tests: N regressions in parallel
pages.summary: N excess-return regressions; joint null H0: α1=...=αN=0; stack α̂. Individual t-tests ignore cross-equation residual correlation ⟹ need the joint test with full Σ̂.

pages.title: Sampling distribution of α̂
pages.summary: α̂ ~ N(α, (1/T)[1+μ̂m²/σ̂m²]Σ̂). μ̂m, σ̂m² are market excess-return sample moments; Σ̂=(1/T)Σε̂tε̂t'. Higher market Sharpe ⟹ noisier alphas.

pages.title: From t-tests to the joint F
pages.summary: Quadratic form J = α̂'[Var(α̂)]⁻¹α̂. GRS exact small-sample: J1 = [(T−N−1)/N]·α̂'Σ̂⁻¹α̂/(1+μ̂m²/σ̂m²) ~ F(N, T−N−1). Large J1 ⟹ reject.

pages.title: The key identity: a Sharpe-ratio gap
pages.summary: α'Σ⁻¹α = θq² − θm², where q is the in-sample tangency from test assets + benchmark. J1 = [(T−N−1)/N](θq²−θm²)/(1+θm²). Under H0, M is the tangency and J1=0.

pages.title: Geometric interpretation of GRS
pages.summary: Excess-return frontier with rays from the origin: market ray slope θm through interior point M; tangency ray slope θq touching at q. At σ=1 the ray heights are the Sharpes; hypotenuses Od, Oc give J1 = [(T−N−1)/N][(Od/Oc)²−1]. Testing α=0 ⟺ testing M is tangency.

pages.title: The empirical evidence at a glance
pages.summary: Early 1970s (BJS 1972, FM 1973, Blume–Friend): supportive. Late 1970s+: anomalies = characteristics that raise the ex-post Sharpe above the market's (size, BE/ME, leverage, E/P, momentum...). CAPM stays useful as benchmark.

pages.title: FF93: five common risk factors
pages.summary: Stocks: Mkt−rf, SMB, HML. Bonds: TERM (LT gov − T-bill), DEF (LT corp − LT gov). Extensions over FF92: add bonds; add bond factors; time-series tests (loadings = risk sensitivities).

pages.title: Constructing SMB and HML: the 2×3 sort
pages.summary: NYSE-median size split (S/B) × BE/ME 30/70 split (L/M/H) ⟹ 6 VW portfolios. SMB = ⅓(SL+SM+SH) − ⅓(BL+BM+BH); HML = ½(SH+BH) − ½(SL+BL); Corr(SMB,HML)≈0 by construction. NYSE breakpoints, value weights, finer BE/ME sort.

pages.title: Why size and BE/ME?
pages.summary: FF95: high BE/ME = persistently depressed earnings (≥5 yrs); low BE/ME = persistent high earnings; small firms suffer more in recessions. Risk reading: proxies for undiversifiable distress/earnings-cycle shocks.

pages.title: The 32 dependent variables
pages.summary: 25 size×BE/ME stock portfolios (5×5 NYSE-quintile independent sort, VW, rebalanced each June) + 7 bond portfolios (2 gov by maturity; 5 corporate by rating Aaa..LG). Bonds discipline the model: it should price stocks AND bonds.

pages.title: Table 1: summary stats, 25 portfolios
pages.summary: 7/63–12/91, 342 months. Means rise with BE/ME within size (value effect, ≈0.6%/mo in the corner) and fall with size (size effect). Small-growth corner most volatile (σ 7.76).

pages.title: Table 3: TERM and DEF on stocks
pages.summary: Bond factors alone: TERM slopes ≈0.8–1.0, DEF slopes 0.7–1.5, all highly significant (t 3.6–9.6); DEF loadings largest for small stocks.

pages.title: Table 3: R² and bonds
pages.summary: Bond factors leave stocks mostly unexplained (R² 0.06–0.21) but price bonds superbly (R² 0.97–0.98 top-grade; junk 0.49). Average TERM/DEF premia too small to explain cross-sectional stock spreads.

pages.title: Table 4: market factor alone, stocks
pages.summary: One-factor betas 0.84–1.42, all t>20; R² 0.61–0.92. Real explanatory room remains for size and value.

pages.title: Table 4: market factor on bonds
pages.summary: Bond b small (0.08–0.30) but significant; junk R²=0.29. Stocks and bonds share some market variation, not most.

pages.title: Table 5: SMB and HML alone, stocks
pages.summary: s falls monotonically with size (1.93 small → −0.05 big edge); h rises with BE/ME. Huge t-stats — genuine common variation.

pages.title: Table 5: R² plus bonds
pages.summary: SMB/HML alone: stock R² 0.04–0.65 (big-growth corner unexplained); high-grade bonds load zero; junk s=0.19 (t=4.19).

pages.title: Table 6: three-factor b and s
pages.summary: With Mkt+SMB+HML: market betas collapse toward 1 (0.91–1.18, t up to 65); s declines monotonically with size (1.46→−0.23).

pages.title: Table 6 (cont.): h loadings
pages.summary: h rises monotonically with BE/ME within every size bucket: ≈−0.5 growth to +0.6–0.76 value; |t| up to 25. The defining FF93 pattern.

pages.title: Table 6: R² plus bonds
pages.summary: Three-factor stock R² 0.83–0.97 — the highest yet. Bonds still need TERM/DEF.

pages.title: Table 9a: intercepts, specs (i)-(iii)
pages.summary: Bond-factors-only: intercepts positive everywhere. CAPM: big positive alphas in the high-BE/ME column (value alphas 0.5–0.57, t≈3). SMB+HML without the market: intercepts everywhere (≈0.5, the equity premium leaks in).

pages.title: Table 9a (cont.): 3-factor and 5-factor intercepts
pages.summary: Three-factor alphas tiny except small-growth −0.34 (t −3.16) and big-growth +0.21 (t 3.27); five-factor essentially identical — TERM/DEF absorbed by the stock factors.

pages.title: Table 9c: GRS F on the intercepts
pages.summary: GRS F: bond-only 2.09; CAPM 1.91; SMB+HML 1.78; three-factor 1.56 (smallest); five-factor 1.66. All reject formally, but 3-factor misfit is concentrated in the small-growth corner; elsewhere |α|≲0.20%/mo.

pages.title: Robustness and conclusions
pages.summary: Residual predictability, January seasonals, split-sample factor formation, E/P and D/P sorts. Market factor explains the stock–bond premium; TERM/DEF matter for time-series, not cross-section. Open: why size and BE/ME — risk, mispricing, or data mining?

pages.title: What rejecting the CAPM buys us
pages.summary: CAPM works descriptively, fails quantitatively. Three responses: multifactor models (FF3, Carhart, FF5); the tests are flawed (Roll, conditioning, selection); behavioral (mispricing + limits to arbitrage). CAPM remains the benchmark.

pages.title: Cross-sectional and time-series tests: summary
pages.summary: FM 1973: month-by-month cross-sections, average the slopes; issues: EIV, microstructure. FF92: beta dead, size & BE/ME live. GRS 1989: joint α=0 ⟺ M mean–variance efficient (Sharpe-gap geometry). FF93: three factors capture most of the cross-section. Big picture: every asset pricing test asks whether SOME portfolio is MV-efficient.
